contrast: N/A (no neuroimaging)
sample_size: N = 188 recruited; N = 128 after excluding groups with drop-out (mean age: 38.5 ± 12.7 SD; 44 females). Online experiment via Prolific.
ecological_validity: The socially correlated bandit improves on previous paradigms by introducing personalized but correlated rewards, mimicking real-world settings where social information must be adjusted for individual differences (e.g., restaurant reviews, matters of taste). However, the task is still a lab-based grid search with abstract rewards and time pressure (10s choice deadline), limiting naturalistic social interaction. Groups were yoked (not face-to-face) and communication was limited to observing choices/outcomes.
concerns: Conference proceedings paper (6 pages) — relatively brief methods and results. No supplement available. The paper reports evolutionary simulations and behavioral model fitting but does not report neural data. title: Cognitive modeling of socially transmitted affordances: A computational model of behavioral adoption tested against archival data from the Stanford Prison Experiment
study_focus: Social transmission of affordances; observational learning; behavioral adoption; social influence on imitation
study_focus_short: Social transmission of affordances · observational learning
learning_mode_description:
- Learning mode: Learning new behavioral affordances through observation of other agents' actions in a social environment

    - Source content (social): action/policy (observed behaviors — e.g., Throw In Hole, Resist)

task_description: Simulated agents modeled on Stanford Prison Experiment participants (9 prisoners, 10 guards) interacted across 6 simulated days (693 ten-minute steps). Agents observed each other's actions and could learn new behavioral affordances (e.g., Throw In Hole, Resist) through attention-mediated observational learning, then adopt those behaviors based on motivational factors derived from personality.
players: Multi-agent (19 cognitive agents: 9 prisoners + 10 guards), two groups (prisoner group vs guard group)
stimuli: Archival personality data (Comrey Personality Inventory, F-Scale, Mach test) used to parameterize agents; actions coded from video (Command, Help, Information, Insult, Resist, Threaten, Use of Instruments, Throw In Hole); prison schedule activities
main_result:
- Action ordering: Meme Hypothesis condition best predicted the order agents first adopted Throw In Hole (correspondence = 0.85, 0.81 without innovators) — all conditions performed better than chance (0.50)
- Full Knowledge condition best predicted Resist ordering (0.84 without innovators vs Meme 0.61)
- Emotional validation: prisoners 2.3–3.4 times less happy than guards across conditions, matching empirical finding of ~3x difference (t(57.5)=5.70 for Full Knowledge, t(35.2)=116.7 for Authority, t(57.4)=87.0 for Meme; all p < 10^-6)
- Action frequencies: Command, Information, Help matched relative ground-truth rankings; Resistance significantly overrepresented in simulation (0.29–0.30 vs 0.09 ground truth)
- Primary drivers of social learning in Meme condition: valence, selective attention, and in-group membership
effect_size:
- Action ordering correspondence (Throw In Hole): Meme = 0.85, Full Knowledge = 0.82, Authority = 0.67
- Action ordering correspondence (Resist): Full Knowledge = 0.71, Authority = 0.69, Meme = 0.79
- Emotional state: prisoners 2.3–3.4x less happy than guards (t(57.5) = 5.70, t(35.2) = 116.7, t(57.4) = 87.0; all p < 10^-6)
learning_from: Other (guards/prisoners); observed actions and their outcomes in shared environment
learning_about: World; new action affordances (behavioral adoption possibilities)
winning_model: PMFServ cognitive architecture with: attentional salience model (linear weighted sum of 9 cues: novelty, motivated attention, transferability, authority, similarity, valence, in-group, reference group, conformity) → winner-take-all attention → associative memory (exposure-based familiarity) → SEU-based motivation → affordance-based action selection
model_family: Agent-based cognitive architecture (PMFServ); composite of: linear attentional salience model, associative memory with exposure-based familiarity, subjective emotional utility (SEU) decision model, Social Information Model (SIM) for conformity
model_class: Socio-cognitive agent-based model; observational learning; multi-mechanism behavioral adoption

- Authority: structural variable from PMFServ (role-based)
- Similarity: GSP congruence (Eq. 3), distance between personality vectors

- In-group [S]: binary (0/1) — shared group membership
- Reference group [S]: internal membership desire scaled to [0,1]

def_quote: Social learning is one way for this learning to occur. Social learning of affordances is important because the space of possible actions for human interaction is vast. Even easily inferred actions can remain unknown, simply due to competition for attention. Learning by observation greatly reduces this space, exposing an agent to the affordance in practice. Observing such an action can allow an agent to discover an affordance. If affordances are inferred by direct observation, this corresponds to learning by imitation. Alternatively, affordances can be learned indirectly through verbal descriptions and other social mechanisms.
research_question: Can a cognitive agent-based model (extending PMFServ) that integrates attention, social influence, and motivation mechanisms of observational social learning explain and predict how new behaviors (affordances) spread and are adopted among agents, evaluated against archival behavioral data from the Stanford Prison Experiment?
sl_operationalization: Social learning is operationalized as memetic transmission of "hidden affordances" (unknown action opportunities) via observation of others' actions: a cognitive architecture models competition for limited attentional resources (who/what an agent attends to among many possible others), social influence, and motivation to determine whether an agent perceives and then adopts an observed behavior, combining Bandura's Social (Cognitive) Learning Theory with Shannon's information theory; the resulting simulated adoption dynamics are compared against guards' and prisoners' archival behavioral-adoption data from the Stanford Prison Experiment.
sl_framing: uses a related construct without defining social learning (e.g. mentalizing, observational learning, reinforcement learning)
sl_framing_note: Uses "social learning" pervasively but grounds its operative construct in Bandura's Social (Cognitive) Learning Theory/observational learning and "affordance/meme transmission" rather than giving its own explicit stand-alone definition of the term.
agent_constellation_note: 19 simulated cognitive agents (9 prisoners, 10 guards) with an explicit authority/status stratification built directly into the model (initial authority value 0 for prisoners vs. 0.25 for guards), and one of the three tested hypotheses is explicitly named the 'Authority' condition, in which agents are primed by an 'Experimenter' agent with high authority. Rank/status is salient to both the task and the computational model itself, beyond a simple two-group structure, which is why this was coded as Social structure/hierarchy rather than Group.

citation: Panizza, F., Vostroknutov, A., & Coricelli, G. (2021). How conformity can lead to polarised social behaviour. *PLoS Computational Biology*, *17*(10), e1009530. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009530
title: How conformity can lead to polarised social behaviour
study_focus: Social influence learning / norm conformity learning — how observing others' prosocial or antisocial choices polarises one's own social attitude, and whether this is driven by contagion, compliance, preference learning, or norm learning (norm salience).
study_focus_short: Social influence learning / norm conformity learning
learning_mode_description:
- Learning mode: Learning from observed agent's prosocial/antisocial choices about the salience of social norms governing resource allocation
  - Learning from:
    - Source type (social): other (observed agent — individual, group, or computer depending on condition)
    - Source content (social): action/policy (the agent's choices in the resource-allocation game)
  - Learning about:
    - Target type (social): social structure (social norms — how salient norm-following is)
    - Target content (social): state (mental state; normative beliefs about social appropriateness)
task_description: Participants repeatedly chose between a default allocation (100 points to self, 50 to an unknown other) and an alternative allocation that could be more prosocial or antisocial. Halfway through, they predicted the choices of an extremely prosocial or antisocial agent (computer, individual, or group), then resumed making allocation choices.
players: Single agent (participant), single-target (unknown other recipient); between-subjects manipulation of observed agent type (computer / individual / group of 5 / no agent baseline). N = 369 across 4 conditions.
stimuli: Point allocations on a circumference (self vs. other trade-offs), binary choice (alternative vs. default allocation), feedback on prediction accuracy during manipulation phase.
main_result:
- Participants polarised their social attitude toward the observed agent's extreme attitude across Computer, Individual, and Group conditions (all p < .001) but not Baseline (p = .457)
- Attitude convergence in the Computer condition was driven by authority compliance (interaction: β = 25.31, t = 4.70, p < .001), not by contagion
- After removing compliant participants, attitude convergence remained significant in Individual (r = .57) and Group (r = .55) conditions but weakened in Computer condition (r = .30)
- No evidence for preference learning hypothesis (no differential increase in consistency between human vs. non-human conditions; BF_01 favoured null for most comparisons)
- Norm elicitation showed prosocial and antisocial participants had different normative beliefs (all p < .004), supporting norm learning
- No evidence for norm uncertainty (67/72 Bayes Factor tests favoured null); norm salience was the surviving explanation
- Variable Attitude model (both α and σ vary) won model comparison (DIC_VA = 32997.4)
effect_size:
- Attitude convergence Computer condition: r = .43 [.23, .63], BF_+0 = 786.20
- Attitude convergence Individual condition: r = .57 [.41, .75], BF_+0 > 10000
- Attitude convergence Group condition: r = .58 [.43, .72], BF_+0 > 10000
- Baseline vs. Group: r = −.39 [−.51, −.27], BF_10 > 10000
- Compliance × Computer interaction: β = 25.31 [14.75, 35.87], t = 4.70
- Group condition main effect: β = 4.67 [3.29, 6.03], t = 6.67
- Individual condition main effect: β = 3.69 [1.89, 5.50], t = 4.011
- Compliance index vs. κ_before: ρ = .62 [.55, .67]
- Model comparison adjusted R² = .241
learning_from: Other (observed agent's choices in resource-allocation game — computer, individual, or group); source: other / group
learning_about: Social norms (how salient norm-following is in the social context); target: social structure / norms
winning_model: Variable Attitude model (full version): V(π_y, π_o) = π_y + tan(α) × π_o, with α ~ N(μ, σ); Pr(D=1) via probit link with threshold T_α; error parameter ε; bias parameter κ. Both α and σ estimated separately before/after manipulation.
model_family: Utility/value function with random preference (probit model with normally distributed social attitude parameter)

v4_study_focus: Whether attitude polarisation after observing an extremely prosocial or antisocial agent in a resource-allocation game reflects contagion, authority compliance, preference learning, or norm learning, tested by manipulating between subjects whether the observed agent is a computer, one previous participant, a group of five, or absent.
v4_coding_notes: Preregistered (osf.io/th6wp). Winning model was the full Variable Attitude (random-preference) model with alpha and sigma free before and after the manipulation phase; the bias parameter kappa correlated with the compliance index (rho = .62). Single study with four between-subjects conditions, coded as one row consistent with the manifest. agent_constellation recorded as Dyadic-observation because in every condition the participant watches a single choosing agent (in the Group condition the agent's choices are the group's modal response); the allocation recipient is a passive third party.

v4_goal_rule_acquisition_desc: Learning what counts as socially appropriate in the allocation game (which norm is in place, and how strictly it is followed), measured afterwards by the incentivised norm-elicitation task rating appropriateness of alternative allocations.

citation: Kim, J., Lee, S. W., Yoon, S., Park, H., & Jeong, B. (2021). Neurocomputational mechanism of controllability inference under a multi-agent setting. *PLoS Computational Biology*, *17*(11), e1009549. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009549
title: Neurocomputational mechanism of controllability inference under a multi-agent setting
study_focus: Controllability inference learning — how agents infer their own controllability over outcomes in a multi-agent setting by integrating self and other action-outcome contingencies via Bayesian inference.
learning_mode_description:
- Learning mode: Learning from both one's own and another agent's action-outcome contingencies to infer who controls the shared outcome
  - Learning from:
    - Source type (non-social): self
      - Source content (non-social): outcome (reward/loss from shared task)
    - Source type (social): other (partner/artificial agent)
      - Source content (social): outcome (other's action-outcome contingency)
  - Learning about:
    - Target type (social): self (relative to other)
      - Target content (social): state (mental state; controllability belief — who is the causal controller)
task_description: Two participants (actually participant vs. artificial RL agent) simultaneously make binary choices; only one person's choice determines the shared outcome (reward or loss, 80/20 probability). The controller switches every 20-30 trials, and participants must infer who currently controls the outcome using both their own and the other's action-outcome history.
players: Single agent (participant), dyadic (artificial RL agent presented as another participant)
stimuli: Abstract two-alternative choice options, binary feedback (reward/loss), other's choice display
main_result:
- Correlated own action-outcome increased perceived controllability (beta = 1.48, t = 11.91)
- Correlated other's action-outcome decreased perceived controllability (beta = -1.78, t = -15.04)
- Reward biased controllability perception toward self (d = 0.901)
- Perceived controllability increased optimal choices (d = 0.481)
- Positive bias (bias_pos) significantly > 0 (d = 0.441); negative bias (bias_neg) significantly < 0 (d = -0.495)
- Controllability-dependent value utilization parameter tau significantly > 0 (d = 0.854)
- Positive bias correlated with illusion of control (r_partial = 0.39) and choice optimality in second half of self-controllable blocks (r_partial = 0.26)
- Low positive bias and high negative bias associated with daily guilt (r_partial = 0.27 for bias_neg with guilt; r_partial = -0.25 for bias_pos with guilt)
- TPJ and striatum covaried with log-controllability ratio (LCR): left TPJ [-50, -22, 26], Z = 4.37, cluster FWE p = 0.032; right striatum [18, 8, -6], Z = 4.82, cluster FWE p < 0.001
- vmPFC encoded value difference: [0, 52, -12], Z = 5.18, cluster FWE p < 0.001
- vmPFC value signal amplified by predicted controllability: [-2, 34, -14], Z = 4.01, SVC p = 0.012
effect_size:
- Reward vs loss controllability perception: d = 0.901
- Perceived controllability on optimal choice: d = 0.481
- Positive bias (bias_pos): d = 0.441
- Negative bias (bias_neg): d = -0.495
- Value utilization (tau): d = 0.854
- Positive bias vs illusion of control: r_partial = 0.39
- Positive bias vs choice optimality (2nd half): r_partial = 0.26
- Negative bias vs guilt: r_partial = 0.27
- Positive bias vs guilt: r_partial = -0.25
- Controllability signal timing striatum: d = 0.702
- Controllability signal timing TPJ: d = 0.486
- vmPFC interaction vs tau: r_partial = 0.38
learning_from: Self and other's action-outcome contingency (both agents' choices and shared outcomes)
learning_about: Self; controllability state (who is the causal controller of the shared outcome)
winning_model: Multi-Agent Bayesian Controllability (MABC) with reward biases and controllability-guided value utilization (Model 12). Posterior controllability = [exp(bias) * self-likelihood * prior_self] / [exp(bias) * self-likelihood * prior_self + other-likelihood * prior_other]; likelihoods learned via Rescorla-Wagner rule ($\alpha_{self}$, $\alpha_{other}$); value utilization modulated by predicted controllability ($\tau$); drift parameter ($\theta$). 7 free parameters: $\alpha_{self}$, $\alpha_{other}$, $\beta_0$, $\beta_{con}$, bias_{pos}, bias_{neg}, $\tau$, $\theta$.
all_models_tested:
31 computational models compared. The paper describes model space in S2A Fig. Key models include:
- Model 4: Single-agent controllability (self-only, no other-likelihood)
- Model 12 (winning): MABC with bias + controllability-induced value utilization (PEP = 1)
- Various combinations of: multi-agent vs single-agent, with/without bias, with/without controllability-dependent value utilization, with/without drift

Note: Full list of 31 models described in supplementary S2A Fig (not accessible as separate supplement file).
model_params:
- $\alpha_{self}$: learning rate for self action-outcome contingency
- $\alpha_{other}$ [S]: learning rate for other's action-outcome contingency
- $\beta_0$: baseline inverse temperature for outcome-related choices
- $\beta_{con}$: inverse temperature for causality choices
- bias_{pos} [S]: reward-driven bias amplifying self-likelihood relative to other-likelihood after reward (mean significantly > 0, d = 0.441)
- bias_{neg} [S]: loss-driven bias on self-likelihood relative to other-likelihood after loss (mean significantly < 0, d = -0.495)
- $\tau$: controllability-dependent value utilization modulation parameter (mean significantly > 0, d = 0.854)
- $\theta$: drift parameter linking trial-to-trial controllability inference to prediction
social_param: bias_{pos} and bias_{neg} — outcome-valence-dependent biases that differentially weight self-likelihood versus other-likelihood in multi-agent controllability inference. $\alpha_{other}$ — learning rate for other's action-outcome contingency.
model_comparison_metric: Protected exceedance probability (PEP) from random-effects Bayesian model selection (RFX-BMS) using negative variational free energy (Laplace approximation of log model evidence).
how_model_fit: individual-level-fit (variational Bayesian scheme via TAPAS toolbox; MAP estimation with quasi-Newton optimization)
data_type_fit_to:
choice behavior (both outcome-related choices and causality choices jointly)

### QUALITY
sample_size: N = 103 (behavioural; 32 females, mean age 23.8 +/- 2.7 years); N = 30 (fMRI subsample; 8 females, mean age 24.0 +/- 2.7 years)
ecological_validity: Limited — participants believed they played with a real partner but actually interacted with an artificial RL agent; binary choice task with simple reward/loss outcomes; controllability structure (only one person controls) is simplified relative to real-world multi-agent settings where cooperative or partial control is common.
concerns:
- Participants interacted with an artificial RL agent, not a real person (deception paradigm; flagged as automated social agent)
- Both task sets started with a self-controllable block, potentially creating order effects (acknowledged by authors)
- fMRI subsample relatively small (N=30)
- Granger causality analysis has limitations for inferring effective connectivity (acknowledged by authors)
- Supplement tables (S1, S2, S3) referenced for full coordinates and model parameters but supplement file not separately available as text — some coordinate details from S3 Table and S6 Fig could not be verified
limitations_reported: Task assumes only one person controls outcome, whereas real-world situations involve cooperative or no-control scenarios; both task sets started with self-controllable block creating potential blocking effect; Granger causality does not establish effective connectivity; model may be unrealistic with large numbers of agents (>10) because it assumes simultaneous updating of all agents' contingencies; study design does not distinguish whether guilt arises from causing loss to other vs. to self.
limitations_categorized: task simplicity; limited ecological validity; order effects; limited generalizability (model scalability); method limitations (Granger causality); design confound (guilt attribution ambiguity)

v4_topic_note: The stated question is how an agent infers its own controllability over a shared outcome when another agent could also be causing it, which is credit assignment between self and other (the causality choice asks literally who caused the outcome). The controller switched every 20-30 trials and the paper analyses adaptation under this volatile controllability, so uncertainty/change is a second, explicitly studied dimension.
v4_partner_type_desc: Participants believed they were playing simultaneously with another participant in a separate room, but the partner was an artificial reinforcement-learning agent throughout.
v4_setting_desc: In-person testing at KAIST; N=103 behavioural, N=30 of them scanned with fMRI; questionnaires (TOSCA-3) and mood probes administered during the session.
v4_recipient_desc: Both players' choices fed into a single shared outcome (reward or loss) that was the only common element for the pair, so the outcome at stake was joint even though only one person controlled it in a given block.
v4_study_focus: How people infer their own controllability over a shared outcome in a two-agent task by integrating their own and the other agent's action-outcome contingencies, and how the resulting biased Bayesian estimate drives value utilisation (striatum, TPJ, vmPFC) when the true controller switches every 20-30 trials.
v4_coding_notes: Winning model among 31 was the multi-agent Bayesian controllability (MABC) model with reward-driven bias parameters and controllability-guided value utilisation (PEP = 1). Manifest study_focus is accurate.
v4_goal_prediction_desc: Learning p(outcome | action) for oneself and for the other player through a static-learning-rate RL rule, in order to predict which option yields reward when in control.
v4_goal_inference_desc: Bayesian inference of posterior controllability, i.e. who currently controls the shared outcome, from the ratio of self-likelihood to other-likelihood, reported in the periodic causality choice.
v4_goal_action_policy_desc: Selecting the optimal option; inferred controllability of the previous trial modulated inverse temperature (parameter tau > 0), so predicted control increased value-dependent choice.

sl_operationalization: Participants performed a two-alternative choice task believing they played with another real participant (in fact an artificial RL agent) whose action-outcome contingency changed who had true control over reward/loss every 20-30 trials; the study models this as a multi-agent Bayesian controllability (MABC) inference in which the participant integrates their own action-outcome correlation (CIx_self) together with the observed action-outcome correlation of the other agent (CIx_other) as a biased Bayesian update of posterior controllability, with mediation via TPJ/striatum and downstream motivated behavior in vmPFC.

agent_constellation_note: Two participants simultaneously make binary choices in separate rooms, believing they are playing with each other in real time (actually one is an artificial RL agent); only one of them controls the shared outcome at a time, and controllership switches, so both agents' actions jointly determine trial outcomes -- a live two-agent exchange even though the 'other' was algorithmic.

- Learning mode: Learning from reward outcomes on a social decision-tree task about which action sequences maximize social influence points, with social cues (avatars) acting as Pavlovian influences on choice and vigor.

task_description: Participants were told they had recently moved to a fictional town and had to accumulate 'social influence points' by choosing sequences of six actions (each a socially framed activity with a named avatar) per epoch over 40 epochs, from a randomized start location in a six-location, twelve-action decision tree with deterministic transitions and fixed outcomes (+180/+100/+20/-20/-100). Before the task they underwent a validated 4.5-minute image-plus-music affect induction (positive, negative or neutral), with affect grid ratings taken immediately before and after.
players: Single agent (participant), multi-target (fictional townspeople avatars)
stimuli: Avatars of fictional townspeople, social action labels (e.g., "Grocery shop with Aniyah"), nonsocial action labels, affective images from IAPS with mood-congruent music, social influence points as feedback.
main_result:
- SARSA was the preferred cRL model of behavior (EP = 0.993 in Study 1)
- Participants exhibited a Pavlovian bias toward social actions (z = 9.25, p < .001) and sensitivity to immediate value (z = 46.70, p < .001)
- Negative affect induction amplified multiplicative effect of immediate x future value on vigor (t = 2.07, p = .038)
- Negative urgency heightened sensitivity to immediate value and blunted future value influence on choice (z = 2.05, p = .040)
- Negative urgency amplified vigorous pursuit of immediate rewards late in epoch (t = -2.46, p = .014)

- Negative urgency and BPD symptoms predicted affect-dependent alterations for negative and neutral (but not positive) affect inductions

sample_size: N = 388 analyzed (404 completed; 16 excluded for incomplete questionnaires, random responding or failed attention checks); 217 female, 163 male, 8 nonbinary/other; mean age 38 (SD = 13, range 18-84); 76% non-Hispanic White. Randomized to affect induction: positive n = 127, negative n = 134, neutral n = 127. Parameter analyses restricted to the N = 350 with adequate model fit (R^2 > 0.6; 38 excluded).
ecological_validity: Online Prolific community sample with dimensional personality measures rather than clinical BPD sample. Task uses a fictional scenario (moving to a new town, earning "social influence points") with avatar-based social interactions, which is relatively abstract. Affect inductions used validated IAPS images + music. The social component is simulated (no real social interaction), limiting ecological validity for interpersonal processes in BPD. However, the dimensional approach is theoretically well-justified and the task cleverly dissociates Pavlovian vs. goal-directed influences.
eligibility_flag: FLAG: thesis; borderline social learning (social cues present as Pavlovian stimuli but no genuine social interaction or learning from others' behavior); learning does occur over time (40 epochs of trial-and-error learning). | Sociality is a framing manipulation (avatars and socially labeled actions with 'social influence points') rather than a real or believed social partner; the social/nonsocial action distinction is nonetheless built into the winning model's discount parameters. Flag the framing-only sociality. Dissertation - mark publication_type = thesis.
concerns:
- The social element of the task is limited to social cues (avatars, action labels) rather than genuine social interaction; whether this qualifies as "social learning" vs. "learning with social cues" is debatable.
- SARSA-el SS won model comparison in Study 1 (EP = 0.983) but was equivocal in Study 2 (EP = 0.48 vs. SARSA-el EP = 0.41); the same model was used in Study 2 for comparability rather than because it was clearly best.
- Many effects were observed in only one study (Study 1 or Study 2 but not both), raising concerns about replicability.
- Community sample with self-report BPD measures; no clinical diagnosis.
- No parameter recovery or model recovery analyses reported.
- Mean fitted parameter values not accessible from the text extraction (Tables 6-7 referenced but not readable).
- No formal simulation of the winning model prior to fitting (simulation was done for task design validation, not for model validation per Wilson & Collins guidelines).
- The number of statistical tests is very large with no correction for multiple comparisons.
limitations_reported: Community sample relied on self-report measures of personality and psychopathology rather than clinical diagnosis; cannot make inferences about clinical BPD sample; three affect inductions did not produce statistically similar increases in arousal (positive induction did not change arousal, neutral induction decreased arousal); best-fitting model was SARSA rather than the expected mixed MB/MF model, so discounting of future value was not explained by pruning as predicted; differences in task design from prior decision-tree tasks (fixed 6-move epoch, no pre-planning of full action sequence) may account for the preference for SARSA over full model-based models.
limitations_categorized: limited generalizability; limited ecological validity; self-report measures only; no clinical sample; affect manipulation not perfectly controlled; unexpected model selection outcome; task simplicity; no parameter recovery; no model recovery; multiple comparisons not corrected.

v4_goal_action_policy_desc: Choosing one of two available actions at each of six moves per epoch, across 40 epochs, so as to maximize accumulated social influence points.

### CANNOT FIND
- No supplement available to check for additional modeling details or coordinates
- No effect sizes in standard format (Cohen's d, r, etc.) reported for behavioral effects; only F-statistics, Wilcoxon signed ranks, and t-values from fMRI
- No data or code sharing information

### OTHER NOTES
- This paper is primarily about how pre-existing inherent value (facial attractiveness) modulates standard reinforcement learning, rather than about learning in a social context per se. The social element is the use of faces as stimuli with inherent value, not social interaction or learning about others.
- The novel contribution is identifying neural correlates of decaying learning rates in ventral caudate and demonstrating that the multiplicative combination of LR and RPE BOLD signals (via PPI) activates vmPFC regions encoding expected value, providing neural evidence for the Rescorla-Wagner update rule.
- 44 models is an unusually thorough model comparison space.
- The paper was published in J. Neuroscience in 2016.

## QUALITY
sample_size: N = 15 (16 scanned, 1 excluded for incomplete session; ages 18–32; 10 female)
ecological_validity: Low-moderate. The student was actually a computer replaying pre-programmed responses, eliminating genuine social interaction. The teaching context (arbitrary stimulus-response associations) is abstract and does not capture the richness of real-world teaching. However, the cover story was maintained (no participants detected the deception).
concerns:
- Very small sample size (N = 15) limits statistical power and generalizability
- Only one computational model tested; no model comparison possible due to design (all teachers observed same student behavior)
- Student behavior was computer-controlled, not a real interacting partner — limits ecological validity of "teaching"
- The R-W model was fit to the student's behavior and then used to examine the teacher's brain; the teacher's own computational process is inferred, not directly modeled
- Several key neuroimaging results (VTA, caudate, outcome-event PE regions) reported only at uncorrected thresholds
- Individual differences analysis underpowered (N = 15) and reported at uncorrected threshold
- Parameters fitted via grid search rather than optimization; potential for imprecise parameter estimates
limitations_reported: Authors acknowledge: the task design was suboptimal for comparing processing of one's own versus others' actions; the study cannot determine whether ACCg PE signals reflect fictive PEs; results on individual differences should be interpreted with caution given the low sample size and uncorrected thresholds; model comparison could not be meaningfully applied to a single subject's data.
limitations_categorized: Task simplicity; limited ecological validity; sample size; no model comparison; suboptimal task design for some contrasts; uncorrected thresholds for secondary analyses
preregistered:
Not reported

title: Value-related neuronal responses in the human amygdala during observational learning
study_focus: Observational learning — investigating whether human amygdala neurons encode reinforcement learning variables (expected values, outcomes, prediction errors) during learning through observation of another agent's experiences.
learning_mode_description:
- Learning mode: Learning the value of stimuli by observing outcomes experienced by another agent interacting with those stimuli (vicarious/observational reinforcement learning)

    - Target type (non-social): world (stimulus/bandit reward value)

task_description: Neurosurgical patients performed a multi-armed bandit task with 288 trials across interleaved experiential and observational blocks; in observational blocks, participants watched a pre-recorded video of another person experiencing outcomes from bandits (whose rewards were not added to the participant's total), then made binary choices between bandits to test learned values.
players: Single agent (neurosurgical patient), single observed target (pre-recorded video of another person)
stimuli: Colored one-armed bandits (slot machines), point outcomes drawn from normal distributions (truncated at -50 and 150), pre-recorded video of another player's head watching bandit outcomes
main_result:
- Counterfactual RL model with single learning rate best explained behavior (protected exceedance probability = 99.9% over split-LR counterfactual model)
- No significant difference between experiential and observational choice accuracy (p = 0.66, two-sample t-test; overall proportion correct = 0.776 +/- 0.038)
- 9.4% of amygdala neurons sensitive to experiential EV (p < 0.006, permutation test)
- 8.9% of amygdala neurons sensitive to observational EV (p < 0.002, permutation test)
- 10.8% of amygdala neurons sensitive to experiential outcomes (p < 0.002, permutation test)
- Trial type (experiential vs. observational) decoded from amygdala population at 86.1% accuracy (p < 0.002)
- Experiential EV decoded at 36.4% (p < 0.002); observational EV decoding not significant (p < 0.08)
- Experiential outcome decoded at 39.3% (p < 0.002); observational outcome decoded at 33.1% (p < 0.026)
- Cross-condition generalization decoding failed in both directions, and Pearson correlations between experiential and observational sensitivities were non-significant (EV: r = 0.10, p = 0.14; outcome: r = 0.02, p = 0.77), suggesting distinct neuronal populations for observational vs. experiential value coding

- Observational EV unit proportion: 8.9% (18/202 neurons)

- Observational outcome unit proportion: 4.9% (10/202 neurons)

- Experiential EV decoding accuracy: 36.4%
- Observational outcome decoding accuracy: 33.1%
- EV cross-condition sensitivity correlation: r = 0.10
- Outcome cross-condition sensitivity correlation: r = 0.02

learning_about: World; expected value of stimuli (bandits)
winning_model: RL counterfactual (single $\alpha$, 1 $\beta$): both played and unplayed bandits updated on each trial in opposite directions. $V_{chosen}^{t+1} = V_{chosen}^t + \alpha \delta_t$; $V_{unchosen}^{t+1} = V_{unchosen}^t - \alpha \delta_t$; $\delta_t = R_t - V_i^t$

sample_size: N = 12 patients (4 female), neurosurgical epilepsy patients with depth electrodes; 4 patients performed 2 sessions, others 1 session; 14 analyzed sessions (1 pilot excluded, 1 discarded for technical error); 202 single units isolated from amygdala (135 right, 67 left)
ecological_validity: Low ecological validity — observational learning from a pre-recorded video of a stranger's head (not live interaction); Pavlovian paradigm with instrumental choice trials only to test contingency learning; performed in hospital setting with neurosurgical epilepsy patients; authors note the design does not control for social vs. non-social component of OL (the observed agent could be replaced by a computer).
concerns:
- Very small sample size (N = 12 patients, 14 sessions) — typical of intracranial single-neuron studies but limits generalizability
- Epilepsy patient population may not be representative of healthy cognition

- Design does not disentangle social vs. non-social components of observational learning (acknowledged by authors)
- Blocked design (experiential vs. observational blocks) confounds trial type decoding with block-level differences
- Observed agent rewards not added to participant total — no interdependence between agents
- RPE was not significantly encoded or decoded in amygdala, despite being a core RL variable
- Low inverse temperature parameter ($\beta$ = 0.17) suggests noisy decision-making

task_description: Participants first completed a team game (competitive or cooperative) to learn the social rank (superior vs. inferior) of other players. They then played a multi-round Ultimatum Game as the responder, receiving offers (fair/sub-fair/unfair) from proposers whose rank was established in the preceding task.
players: Single agent (participant as responder), multi-target (24 proposers: 6 superior + 6 inferior in competitive context, 6 superior + 6 inferior in cooperative context)
stimuli: Neutral face photographs (gender-matched), monetary offers (1-10 out of 20 CNY), rank cues (1 star = low rank, 3 stars = high rank)
learning_from: Other (proposer); monetary offer outcomes
learning_about: World; internal fairness norm (expected offer)
winning_model:
Fehr-Schmidt inequality aversion utility model with either RW or Bayesian Observer norm learning (best-fitting model selected per subject per condition). Shared parameters: α (unfairness sensitivity, [0,20]), τ (inverse temperature, [0,10]). RW adds ε (learning rate, [0,1]); BO uses Bayesian updating of μ and σ².

Formula: U(x_t) = x_t − α·max{f_t − x_t, 0}; P(accept) = exp(τ·U(x_t)) / (1 + exp(τ·U(x_t)))

RW norm update: f_t = f_{t-1} + ε(x_t − f_{t-1})
BO norm update: Bayesian updating of μ_t and σ²_t
model_class: Prediction error learning / belief updating (fairness norm adaptation)
all_models_tested:
- M0 (Null model): U(x_t) = x_t; n_params = 1 (τ only); family: utility; metric: LOOIC
- Fehr-Schmidt + RW: U(x_t) = x_t − α·max{f_t − x_t, 0} with RW updating; n_params = 3 (α, τ, ε); family: RW; metric: LOOIC
- Fehr-Schmidt + BO: U(x_t) = x_t − α·max{f_t − x_t, 0} with Bayesian observer updating; n_params = 2 (α, τ; BO uses fixed priors); family: Bayesian; metric: LOOIC
model_params:
- α [0,20]: unfairness sensitivity -- how much utility decreases when offer is below expectation. Inferior condition M = 4.69 (SE = 0.58); Superior condition M = 2.92 (SE = 0.36) [S -- modulated by social rank]
- τ [0,10]: inverse temperature -- decision consistency
- ε [0,1] (RW only): learning rate / adaptation rate for fairness norm
social_param: α (unfairness sensitivity) -- significantly modulated by proposer social rank (greater sensitivity to unfairness from inferior vs. superior proposers; ηp² = 0.29)
model_comparison_metric: LOOIC (leave-one-out information criterion)
how_model_fit: individual-level-fit (Bayesian MCMC via rstan; 4 chains, 8000 iterations each, 4000 warmup)
data_type_fit_to:
choice behavior (accept/reject decisions)

title: Mechanisms of social avoidance learning can explain the emergence of adaptive and arbitrary behavioral traditions in humans
study_focus: Social avoidance learning; faithful copying of a demonstrator's choice under threat of punishment (rewarding punishment omission)
learning_mode_description:
- Learning mode: Learning from observing another individual's action choices about which actions to avoid under threat of punishment
  - Learning from:
    - Source type (social): other (demonstrator)
      - In Experiment 4: chain of real participants
    - Source content (social): action/policy (observed action choices between two options)
  - Learning about:
    - Target type (non-social): world (which action is safe vs. punished)
    - Target content (non-social): action/policy (which action to choose to avoid punishment)
task_description: Wearing shock electrodes calibrated to be 'uncomfortable but not painful', participants observed a computer-controlled demonstrator (presented as a previous participant) choose the same one of two abstract fractals on all 20 observation trials without seeing any consequences, then made 20 choices themselves believing shocks could follow their choices. No shock was ever delivered regardless of choice, so every choice was followed by punishment omission.
players: Single agent (participant), single demonstrator (computerized in Exp 1-3; real prior participant in Exp 4). Experiment 4: multi-agent transmission chain (5 generations x 10 chains, N=50).
stimuli: Abstract fractals (red/green color hue), mild electric shocks (100 ms DC-pulse), "$" symbol for reward condition (Exp 2).
main_result:
- Main Results:
  - Exp 1 (punishment omission): Strong behavior copying under threat of punishment (beta = 3.66, SE = 1.14, 95% CI [1.46, 5.89])
  - Exp 2 (reward omission): No significant copying when reward was omitted instead (beta = 0.35, SE = 0.42, 95% CI [-0.48, 1.17])
  - Exp 3 (random punishment): Significant copying even when demonstrated action was randomly punished (beta = 0.75, SE = 0.28, 95% CI [0.2, 1.3])
  - Exp 4 (transmission chain): Behavior transmitted across 5 generations (beta = 3.22, SE = 1.1, 95% CI [1.06, 5.36]); intergenerational correlation r(48) = .35
  - RPO parameter correlated with P(A): r(23) = -0.49
  - Social learning rate correlated with P(A): r(23) = 0.59
  - Stronger repeat-choice tendency under punishment threat vs. reward omission (Exp 1 vs. Exp 2 interaction: beta = 5.30, SE = 1.71, z = 4.09)
effect_size: beta = 3.66 (Exp 1); beta = 0.35 (Exp 2, n.s.); beta = 0.75 (Exp 3); beta = 3.22 (Exp 4); r = .35 (intergenerational transmission); r = -0.49 (RPO-P(A) correlation); r = 0.59 (social LR-P(A) correlation)
learning_from: Other (demonstrator); observed action choices (no outcome information visible).
learning_about: World; which action to select to avoid punishment.
winning_model: Individual-level RL combining behavior copying and rewarding punishment omission: Q(t+1) = Q(t) + alpha_I x delta(t) with delta(t) = R(t) - Q(t) for own experience, and Q(t+1) = Q(t) + alpha_O x delta(t) with delta(t) = 1 - Q(t) for observed demonstrator choices; fitted per participant by maximum-likelihood optimization. Estimated omission/punishment-value parameter and alpha_O correlated with individual P(A) (r(23) = -0.49 and 0.59).

research_question: How can rare or nonexistent objective punishment nonetheless give rise to and sustain avoidance "traditions" in groups? sl_operationalization: An agent-based reinforcement-learning simulation in which each simulated agent, before choosing between two actions under threat of punishment, observes M choices of a randomly selected "demonstrator" agent and updates the observed action's expected value via a social learning rate parameter (α_O, scaling a "social prediction error" between the demonstrator's observed and expected behavior); this is combined across generations with an individual learning rate (α_I) and an RPO sensitivity parameter (ρ). sample_size: N = 50 (25 women) = 10 chains x 5 generations; separate sample.
ecological_validity: Low-moderate. Uses abstract fractal stimuli and electric shock as punishment currency, which is far from naturalistic social norms and taboos. The transmission chain (Exp 4) captures some aspects of intergenerational cultural transmission but is limited to 5 generations and binary choices. The authors acknowledge that experimental tests are restricted to brief timescales and a single punishment currency (electric shocks). The computerized demonstrator in Exp 1-3 removes natural variability in social information.
eligibility_flag: Unlike Exps 1-3 the demonstrator from generation 2 onward is a real prior participant, so no automated-agent flag applies beyond generation 1. Note that the unit of transmission analysis is the chain (n = 10), which is small for the generation-level inferential statistics.
concerns: (1) Only one model tested -- no formal model comparison with alternative models (e.g., model-based RL, conformity models). (2) Supplement referenced for parameter estimates (Supplemental Table 1) and sensitivity analyses but supplement not accessible for verification. (3) Mean fitted parameter values not reported in main text. (4) The "threat of punishment" is an auxiliary assumption not explicitly modeled -- participants were simply instructed they might receive shocks. (5) Agent-based simulation uses fixed parameter values rather than fitted; correspondence between simulation and experimental models is qualitative rather than quantitative.
limitations_reported: The experimental investigation is limited to a specific timescale (brief) and a punishment currency (electric shocks); the discrepancy between theoretical scope and experimental investigations is acknowledged; the model represents the simplest computational implementation and alternative representational accounts (model-based RL) could produce identical behavioral predictions; the agent-based model did not include heritable traits or strategic interaction; network-based transmission biases were not modeled; the focus on direct observation excludes verbal/symbolic social learning; results may not generalize to situations with external rewards.

def_quote: Avoidance learning is a form of instrumental learning [28] describing how the likelihood of performing certain behaviours is diminished through experiencing stressful or unpleasant events [28,29] and is naturally present in social interaction [30].
research_question: How do people gradually learn to optimize their facial expressions (smiling/frowning) during dyadic interactive exchanges with dynamic facial stimuli, and what computational (RL/DDM) mechanisms underlie this learning and the accompanying decision process, including adaptation to a mid-experiment reversal of reinforcement contingencies?
sl_operationalization: Participants interacted with dynamic facial stimuli (smiling/frowning "target interactants") and, on each trial, chose to smile or frown back; correct/incorrect facial responses (reciprocating or opposing the target's expression) were reinforced via presence/absence of a mild aversive shock, with contingencies reversed halfway through. Learning is operationalized as trial-by-trial Rescorla-Wagner-style value updating (compared against copy-bias and expression-bias RL variants) of the expected value of smiling vs. frowning toward each individual target interactant, combined with a drift diffusion model of the choice/RT process.
sl_framing: uses a related construct without defining social learning (e.g. mentalizing, observational learning, reinforcement learning)
sl_framing_note: The phrase "social learning" never appears in the text; the authors instead frame the phenomenon explicitly as reinforcement learning (Rescorla-Wagner) and instrumental/avoidance learning occurring within a social/interactive dyadic context.
agent_constellation_note: Participant views one pre-recorded dynamic-face video (target interactant) per trial and reacts (smile/frown) to avoid shock; the target interactant is a fixed video and does not respond live to the participant's behavior, so each encounter is a passive one-on-one observation-and-react exchange. There are two distinct target interactants overall (one congruent, one incongruent condition), encountered on separate trials rather than simultaneously, which is why Dyadic-observation (rather than Group) was chosen.

main_result:
- Main Results:

  - Emulation propensity predicted F1 after controlling for age, gender, cognitive ability (beta = -0.264, eta-p-squared = 0.0696)
  - Emulation bias predicted F1 after controlling for all model parameters (beta = -0.130, eta-p-squared = 0.0165)

- Emulation bias ~ F1: r = -0.124

sample_size: Study 1: N=943 (after exclusion from initial N=1197; 500 females, 435 males, 7 nonbinary; age = 37.20 +/- 12.19); recruited from MTurk (1028) and Prolific (169)
ecological_validity: Online observational learning task (~15 min) with pre-recorded partner videos; reasonable ecological validity for observational learning but partner is not a real-time interactive agent; social interaction is limited to observing pre-recorded choices. concerns: (1) SRS total scores were inflated relative to normative samples, possibly due to COVID-19 pandemic effects and online sample characteristics -- authors addressed this with factor analysis but the resulting Factor 1 measure is an approximation of autism-like traits, not equivalent to validated clinical measures. (2) The partner is a pre-recorded agent, not a real interactive partner, limiting the social dimension. (3) Study 1 had asymmetric task design where emulation led to higher accuracy, confounding emulation propensity with general cognitive ability (addressed in Study 2). (4) No neuroimaging data.
limitations_reported: We mainly relied on the SRS to measure autistic traits while several other widely applied measurements such as the 50-item Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) and 36-item Broad Autism Phenotype Questionnaire (BAPQ) may provide more robust measures with greater specificity to autism"; "data in Study 1 was collected at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic and during the height of lockdowns... may have caused a subset of items relating to direct social interactions to be overscored"; "both studies were conducted online, and it is possible that online participants have different personality and behavior profiles compared to people who come to the lab for in-person studies"; "it is still unclear from our data whether imitation is affected (either strengthened or impaired) by heightened autism-like traits"; "the current task was designed to separate imitation and emulation rather than optimize arbitration
limitations_categorized: Measurement validity (self-report scale confounds); limited ecological validity (COVID-era data collection, online sample); task simplicity (not optimized for arbitration measurement); limited generalizability (general population, not clinical ASD sample)
preregistered:
No (Study 1 exploratory; Study 2 described as "confirmatory" replication but not formally preregistered)

def_quote: Therefore, individuals often learn about the world and optimize their behavior by observing others' behaviors and making inferences from social cues. Observational learning can be used even in the absence of observable outcomes, in which case two strategies can be deployed. The first strategy is goal emulation, in which the observer makes active inferences about the observee's beliefs and the environment from their behaviors, and selects actions that are most consistent with the observee's inferred goal. The second strategy is action imitation, in which the observer repeats the observed actions without inferring the underlying goal.

## QUALITY
sample_size: N=29 (30 recruited, 1 dropped due to anxiety; mean age 22.97 +/- 0.37 years; 14 women; all right-handed)
ecological_validity: Lab-based economic game with computer-simulated partners (participants believed they were playing with real humans). Abstract monetary incentives; limited ecological validity as real-world group decisions involve richer social cues, non-anonymous interactions, and varied group sizes. However, the volunteer's dilemma paradigm captures a meaningful real-world social dilemma (e.g., bystander intervention, blood donation).
concerns: Participants played with computer-simulated partners, not real humans, which may alter social reasoning; the authors mention this but the deception could affect generalizability. No neuroimaging data despite the paper's framing as relevant to social neuroscience. Effect sizes (Cohen's d, eta-squared, etc.) are not reported — only t-statistics and CIs. The I-POMDP comparison is relegated entirely to supplement (which is not accessible as a separate file). No parameter recovery or model recovery analyses reported.
limitations_reported: Mimicking human behavior does not guarantee that a POMDP model (or any model) is being implemented in the brain"; model based on binomial/beta distributions specific to binary task structure; framework assumes same prior across games for each subject; no exploration-exploitation trade-off modeled; extension to non-anonymous settings would incur significant computational cost; data and code available upon request only (not openly shared)

## QUALITY
sample_size: N = 173 (28 vmPFC lesion patients, ages 37-76, mean = 57, 15 females; 21 lesion controls, ages 28-74, mean = 56, 13 females; 124 healthy controls, ages 20-80, mean = 53, 71 females). Groups matched on age, gender, empathy; vmPFC group matched to both controls on cognitive ability and apathy.
ecological_validity: Laboratory-based task with abstract symbols and binary feedback; deception procedure used to create belief in anonymous other participant (confederate); ecological validity limited by abstract stimuli and lack of real social interaction, though the monetary incentive structure and role-assignment procedure enhance motivational realism.
concerns:
- Mean fitted parameter values not reported (only group comparisons of parameters)
- Lesion patients have natural lesions with correlated voxel damage patterns, potentially biasing localization
- No one condition interpreted as "non-social control" but could also index hypothetical vs. real reward distinction
- Lesion maps were mirrored (no laterality hypothesis), which precludes detection of lateralized effects
- VLSM restricted mostly to vmPFC due to voxel inclusion threshold (>= 5 patients), limiting detection of subcortical contributions
limitations_reported: Both social behaviours and reinforcement learning rely on large networks of interconnected cortical and subcortical regions; the study investigated location of function within vmPFC but did not examine how these regions interact during prosocial learning; lesion mapping analyses could reveal additional areas of specialisation with a larger sample; considerable variability in the structure of vmPFC between individuals means sharp anatomical boundaries cannot be confirmed; reliance on natural lesions caused by vascular or haemorrhagic pathology leads to correlations among voxels that can bias estimated locations; no predefined hypothesis about lateralisation so lesions were mirrored; future studies with larger samples needed to investigate functional lateralisation; more complex learning tasks with forgetting rates could assess whether prosocial learning impairments become more pronounced.
limitations_categorized: Limited network-level analysis; sample size (for VLSM subregion detection); individual anatomical variability; lesion correlation structure; lateralization not assessed; task simplicity; limited ecological validity.
flagged_fields:
- model_params mean fitted values: LOW — not reported in main text or supplement; only group-level statistical comparisons available
- model recovery (WC rule 6): HIGH confidence it was NOT done — no mention of model confusion matrix
- preregistered: MEDIUM — not mentioned; likely not preregistered
- coordinates: HIGH — extracted from Supplementary Table 9; note these are VLSM peaks (lesion-symptom mapping), not fMRI activation peaks

NEW_future_directions_reported: Since sgACC activity has been associated with other types of social learning, future studies could examine the causality of sgACC and the role of oxytocin in these processes.; In light of the current findings, it would be interesting to see how deep brain stimulation of the sgACC in patients with depression influences prosocial behaviour and learning.; Novel techniques such as focused ultrasound stimulation could be used to target the sgACC and ACCg and further reveal their respective roles in prosocial learning.; Future studies should also assess whether impairments in prosocial learning differ in more complex learning tasks, for instance when learning about more than two symbols at a time or when having to hold items in working memory.; It would be important for future research to examine how interconnected regions such as the ventral striatum and amygdala interact with vmPFC during prosocial learning.; Future studies with larger samples of patients with focal lesions could investigate functional lateralisation of the vmPFC, particularly the sgACC and ACCg in prosocial learning and decision-making.; It would be important to examine how focal lesions affect the influence of social information such as advice, opinion, and preferences on choices.

title: Abstract cognitive maps of social network structure aid adaptive inference
study_focus: social network structure learning (link prediction from sequential observation)

main_result:
- Main Results:
  - Multistep relational abstraction (Successor Representation) explains schema-like network representations better than triad or community schemas at all values of gamma (BIC comparison; Study 1 simulation + Study 2)
  - Group-level use of SR in Random Walks sample (mean beta = 1.74, t(59) = 6.49, 95% CI = [1.20, 2.27])
  - Group-level use of SR in Paired Associates sample (mean beta = 1.55, t(27) = 6.44, 95% CI = [1.05, 2.04])

  - SR predicts perceived centrality (mean Spearman rho = 0.43)
  - Model correctly predicts individual-level centrality perceptions (18/21 for one pair, 15/21 for another; exact binomial tests P < 0.001 and P = 0.039)

winning_model: Successor Representation with free successor discount gamma and mixture-of-experts weights in a logistic choice rule (individual-level fit, Nelder-Mead, L2-regularised); mean lookahead 5.89 steps (equivalent gamma approx. 0.83); group-level SR weight mean beta = 1.74, t(59) = 6.49

### IMPLEMENTATION LEVEL
sample_size: N = 60 (41 recruited in-lab at Brown, 19 via Prolific; 53 saw 837 random-walk steps, 7 saw 1,674; no demographic data collected; dataset originally collected as a pilot for unrelated experiments and re-analysed here)
ecological_validity: Studies 1-3 use artificial social networks with face stimuli or schematics, limiting ecological validity. Study 4 uses a real-world workplace advice network (21 managers at a technology manufacturing company), providing higher ecological validity but with no control over observational history. The paper itself notes that real-world networks incorporate many uncontrolled sources of knowledge (informal friendships, hierarchy) not provided to the model.
eligibility_flag: None for inclusion; note the sample was an existing pilot dataset re-analysed for this paper, and the outcome measure is a memory/judgement task rather than an incentivised social decision.
concerns:
- Study 1 is a simulation; no human data.
- Studies 3 and 4 are reanalyses of previously published datasets (Sehl et al., 2022; Krackhardt, 1987), not original data collection.
- Random Walks sample (Study 2) was originally collected to pilot unrelated experiments and sample size was unplanned.
- No parameter recovery or model recovery analyses reported.
- The SR model and schema models differ in flexibility (SR has free gamma), making BIC comparisons not fully apples-to-apples for fixed-gamma analyses.
- No formal model comparison metric (e.g., BMS exceedance probability) for the individual-level computational models; PPC used instead.
- Real-world network study (Study 4) requires assumptions about managers' observational history that cannot be verified.
limitations_reported: The SR performs less well for the real-world social network compared to laboratory experiments, likely because real-world networks incorporate other uncontrolled sources of knowledge; memory decay or forgetting may affect fidelity of learned SR in real-world settings; the composition of real-world networks is dynamic and the model assumes a fixed set of individuals; it remains unknown how consciously aware people are of the knowledge structures they build; additional mechanisms may be needed for updating the state space in continually evolving networks.
limitations_categorized: limited ecological validity; memory and forgetting not modeled; static network assumption; limited generalizability to dynamic networks; no neural implementation tested; implicit vs. explicit knowledge not distinguished
flagged_fields:
- model_mb_mf: MEDIUM confidence -- SR is typically described as occupying a middle ground between MB and MF; classified as MF here but the paper itself does not use this terminology
- alpha (learning rate): LOW confidence -- alpha is part of the TD learning rule (Eq. 1) but its fitted value is never reported; it is unclear whether it was fixed or free
- Study 3 model fitting: MEDIUM -- group-averaged synthetic data rather than individual-level fitting

NEW_future_directions_reported: Real-world social networks are constantly evolving, and new individuals joining a social network alter the state space itself, suggesting that an additional mechanism is needed for updating the state space in real-world settings that are continually in flux.; Whether these additional mechanisms interact with learning Successor Representations, or else operate independently, remains an open question.; It also remains unknown how consciously aware people are of the knowledge structures they build through network learning, which has implications for social psychological theories of bias.; A fruitful future direction may be to formally connect multistep abstraction with other kinds of learning abstractions, for example learning that certain social features are indicative of group membership and leveraging this to learn intergroup relations.; How exactly this computation might be instantiated in the brain is presently unclear, though some neural network models of hippocampal learning have converged on comparable solutions.

def_quote: We propose a theory of network representation that explains how people learn inferential cognitive maps of social relations from direct observation, what kinds of knowledge structures emerge as a consequence, and why it can be beneficial to encode systematic biases into social cognitive maps.
research_question: Do people build abstract cognitive maps of social network structure via a single parsimonious "multistep relational abstraction" mechanism (rather than a collection of ad hoc schemas), and does this mechanism support adaptive inference about unobserved relationships (e.g., friendship, trust, advice-giving)?
sl_operationalization: Participants observe direct relational interactions (e.g., a friendship pair via a "Random Walks" or "Paired Associates" sequence of network members) and their evolving mental representation of the network is modeled as a Successor Representation: a temporal-difference reinforcement learning algorithm in which each new one-step observation (e.g., seeing Isa and Asher together) updates beliefs about both that direct link and multistep/indirect links (friends-of-friends, etc.), discounted by parameter gamma. Model fits (varying gamma) to participants' yes/no "are they friends" judgments are compared against fixed schema-based accounts (triad completion, community detection) using BIC.
sl_framing: no explicit framing or discussion of social learning
sl_framing_note: The term "social learning" never appears in the text; the process is framed throughout as learning/building "cognitive maps" of network structure via reinforcement learning (Successor Representation), i.e., as a general abstraction/inference mechanism applied to a social domain, not as "social learning" per se.
agent_constellation_note: Task explicitly requires learning and representing a graph/network structure of pairwise friendships among many network members (13-26 in the artificial networks; 21 real managers in Study 4), and using that network structure to infer unobserved links and trust -- a direct match to the Network category.

title: Neurocomputational mechanisms of confidence in self and others
study_focus: Confidence learning; learning others' ability to compute confidence in others' perceptual decisions (mentalizing learning / trait inference)
learning_mode_description:
- Learning mode: Learning from feedback about another player's choice accuracy to update an estimate of the other player's sensory noise (ability), which is then combined with one's own sensory representation of decision difficulty to compute confidence in the other's choices.

    - Source type (social): other (three other players of varying ability)
      - Not joint

      - Not joint

task_description: Participants viewed random dot motion stimuli and placed post-decision wagers (bets) on perceptual decisions made by either themselves or one of three other players of varying ability (low, medium, high), choosing between a safe guaranteed reward and a risky option contingent on decision accuracy.
players: Single agent (participant), multi-target (3 other players of varying ability: low ~0.55, medium ~0.75, high ~0.95 accuracy)
stimuli: Random dot kinematograms (varying coherence), monetary gamble options (safe vs. risky reward values)
main_result:
- Participants tracked other players' ability and combined it with decision difficulty to guide post-decision wagers (ability on other-trials: t(20) = 4.52, p < .001; ability x type interaction: t(20) = -4.60, p < .001)
- ToM-model (integrating belief state with learned other's sensory noise) outperformed S-model (self-projection) and Q-model (simple value tracking) based on PSIS-LOO and WAIC
- LIP tracked motion coherence on both self- and other-trials but with opposite sign (interaction: t(20) = 3.07, p = .006)
- TPJ encoded model-based confidence estimates selectively on other-trials (confidence on other-trials: t(20) = -2.17, p = .043; confidence on self-trials: t(20) = -0.60, p = .555)
- dmPFC encoded confidence on both trial types in inverse manner (confidence on other-trials: t(20) = -2.67, p = .015; confidence on self-trials: t(20) = 1.79, p = .089)
- Functional connectivity between LIP and TPJ/dmPFC increased on other- vs. self-trials (PPI: TPJ t(20) = 2.50, p = .021; dmPFC t(20) = 2.56, p = .019)
- TPJ and dmPFC tracked social prediction errors (TPJ: t(20) = -3.18, p = .005; dmPFC: t(20) = -3.12, p = .005)
effect_size: Effect sizes reported as t-statistics only (N = 21); no Cohen's d, r, or standardized betas reported for main behavioural or neural effects.

ecological_validity: Low — abstract perceptual task (random dot motion) with pre-created "other players" who were not actually present during scanning. No real-time social interaction. sample_size: N = 16 in the final sample (9 girls, 7 boys; mean age 14.87 months, range 14.00-15.97). A further 11 infants were tested but excluded for experimenter error (2), fussiness (4) or failing to produce a demonstrated action (5).
ecological_validity: Lab-based imitation task with physical toys; fairly naturalistic object-manipulation context for infants, though structured demonstration procedure limits ecological validity. Objects are custom-built experimental toys, not everyday objects.
eligibility_flag: Borderline — the computational model is applied post hoc to qualitatively capture ordinal patterns across conditions. It is not formally fit to individual-level behavioral data (no parameter estimation from data, no quantitative model comparison). The model is a Bayesian categorization model, not a trial-by-trial learning model. Participants are 15-month-old infants, which is unusual for the review corpus. The "learning over time" criterion is marginal — infants observe a few demonstrations and then act once on a test object, which is closer to one-shot generalization than iterative learning. FLAG: borderline computational modeling (qualitative fit only); borderline learning-over-time (few-shot demonstration, single test trial).
concerns:
- The computational model is not formally fit to data — it produces qualitative ordinal predictions that match the pattern of results, but no quantitative fit metrics (BIC, AIC, log-likelihood) are reported
- Cohen's d values of 4.23 and 4.50 in Experiment 1 are implausibly large, likely calculated incorrectly (possibly using SE rather than SD in the denominator, or a non-standard formula)
- No parameter recovery or model recovery performed
- Model is demonstrated on aggregate experimental conditions, not fit to individual participant data
- α is fixed at 1, not estimated; β is learned hierarchically but its fitted values are not reported
- Small sample sizes (N = 16 per experiment for Experiments 1 and 2)
limitations_reported: Cannot determine whether generalization is an object-centered categorical process or an action-centered encoding process; model does not provide precise quantitative fit; features in the model are treated as equally weighted, which may not reflect infant cognition; developmental mechanisms underlying the 12-to-15-month transition in generalization ability are not addressed
limitations_categorized: Model ambiguity (multiple theoretical interpretations); limited quantitative model fit; simplistic feature representation; developmental mechanism unspecified; small sample sizes

title: Human hippocampus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex infer and update latent causes during social interaction
study_focus: Latent-cause inference in social interaction: inferring which of two co-acting characters was responsible for a joint outcome and asymmetrically updating beliefs about their ability (fMRI)
learning_mode_description:
- Learning mode: Inferring which character caused a jointly achieved outcome and updating ability estimates asymmetrically based on inferred responsibility.
  - Learning from:
    - Source type (non-social): world
      - Source content (non-social): outcome (jointly achieved performance score)
  - Learning about:
    - Target type (social): other (fictional characters working in pairs)
      - Target content (social): state (mental state; ability/competence of each character)
task_description: Participants observed an outcome (a score bar) said to have been achieved by a pair of fictional characters working together, then saw the two characters in sequence and judged which was responsible, updating beliefs about each character's ability across trials. Performed inside a 3T MRI scanner alongside a localiser task, in a session of about 80 minutes.
players: Single agent (participant), multi-target (3 fictional characters forming 3 possible pairs)
stimuli: Face images (from Radboud and Basel face databases), numerical performance outcomes displayed as bar on a score frame
main_result:

  - Negative interaction between outcome and |PE| on rating (B = −0.32, SE = 0.03)
  - Positive interaction between PE and responsibility on rating update (B = 0.58, SE = 0.05)
  - HMMKF model best fit to trial-by-trial choice (protected exceedance probability = 0.87)
  - Left hippocampus decoded most likely responsible character at outcome presentation (searchlight MVPA, Z = 2.48, cluster-corrected p < 0.05)
  - Hippocampus RSA: activity pattern correlated with 3D ability space (RHC: W = 398, p = 0.035)
  - Hippocampus encoded probability of responsibility (p) at first character presentation (LHC: p_FDR = 0.003; RHC: p_FDR = 0.011)
  - dmPFC: positive interaction of probability and PE for best character (p_FDR = 0.010); negative interaction for worst character (p_FDR = 0.005)
  - dmPFC-hippocampus PPI: functional connectivity increased as function of |PE| (LHC: p_FDR = 0.003)
  - dmPFC cTBS impaired asymmetric update: interaction of PE x responsibility on rating update significantly lower in dmPFC vs vertex condition (V = 148, p = 0.032)

### QUALITY
sample_size: N = 33 analysed of 37 recruited (4 removed for excessive head motion); mean age 24.55 +/- 5.68, 18 female; all right-handed.
ecological_validity: Moderate lab constraints. Task uses fictional characters with faces performing an abstract collaborative task with numerical outcomes. No real social interaction. However, the task captures a naturalistic problem (credit assignment in groups), and Experiment 3 showed the inference process is spontaneous even without explicit responsibility judgments.
concerns: (1) Supplement (Figures S1–S7, Tables S1–S5) not accessible as a separate file — the main text references these extensively for parameter recovery (Figure S2), additional experiments (Experiments 2 and 3 in Figure S1), coordinate tables (Table S1), and cTBS details (Tables S4, S5). Some details therefore could not be verified. (2) Fitted parameter mean values for the HMMKF model are shown in Figure S2 but not reported numerically in the main text. (3) Left hippocampus MVPA cluster peak coordinates (x, y, z) not explicitly reported as numbers in the main text (only Z-statistic given). (4) Process noise (φ) and observation noise (υ) were fixed at 0.0001 — the authors state results did not depend on these values but no formal sensitivity analysis is reported.
limitations_reported: The authors acknowledge that their approach assumes a known, finite number of latent causes, whereas in other situations there may be an infinite capacity prior requiring additional mechanisms; they recognize that additional mechanisms are likely needed when the number of latent causes is unknown; the study focuses on a situation where participants single out one individual as responsible, which may not generalize to all forms of collaborative credit assignment.
limitations_categorized: Task simplicity (fixed number of latent causes); limited generalizability (single-agent responsibility assignment only); limited ecological validity (fictional characters, no real social interaction)
preregistered:
Not reported

v4_topic_note: The paper states its subject directly: inferring which of two characters who worked together was responsible for a joint outcome (latent-cause inference) and then updating the estimate of that character's ability. The responsibility judgment is credit assignment in a social setting; the rating of each character's ability on a min-max scale is inference of competence as an attribute of a person, which under rule 4 belongs in group 4 rather than in group 1 source credibility.
v4_partner_type_desc: Three fictional characters represented by face images from public databases; their joint outcomes were drawn from three fixed overlapping Gaussian distributions, so no real person's behavior was observed. Participants judged and rated them but never interacted with them.
v4_setting_desc: Single 3T fMRI session of about 80 minutes at the Wellcome Centre for Integrative Neuroimaging, Oxford, comprising the latent social cause inference task and a passive localiser task.
v4_recipient_desc: The outcomes belong to the pairs of characters working together; the participant is a third-party observer whose own payoff is a flat fee plus a performance bonus, not the task outcome itself.
v4_study_focus: fMRI study of how people infer which of two characters who achieved a joint score was responsible for it, and then asymmetrically update their estimate of that character's ability, with an ability reversal introduced in the third block.
v4_coding_notes: N = 33 analysed of 37 recruited (mean age 24.55 +/- 5.68, 18 female). Winning model was a hidden Markov model combined with a Kalman filter (HMMKF; protected exceedance probability = 0.87), which reproduced both the responsibility-dependent and the asymmetric update; a generic Kalman filter and a model-free RL algorithm did not. Hippocampus carried a map-like representation of the three-character ability space (RSA, RHC W = 398, p = 0.035) and encoded the probability that the first character was responsible; dmPFC encoded the PE-by-responsibility interaction and its coupling with left hippocampus scaled with |PE|.
v4_goal_prediction_desc: Predicting the score each character would produce, since the signed and unsigned prediction errors between the observed team score and each character's current ability estimate are what drive the responsibility choice (participants chose the character with the smaller |PE|, B = -1.62, SE = 0.13, p < 0.001).
v4_goal_inference_desc: Inferring which of the two co-acting characters was the latent cause of the observed joint score, decodable from left hippocampal activity at outcome onset before either character appeared.

NEW_future_directions_reported: While our findings can be generalized to any process similar to the social latent-cause inference task, we recognize that additional mechanisms are likely to be needed when there is an infinite capacity prior (when the number of latent causes is unknown).; Latent-cause inference may take place under different assumptions in different contexts, including cases where characters might have synergy and their collaboration constitutes a separate latent cause distinct from what each achieves in isolation.

NEW_intervention_type: continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS/TMS) to dmPFC
NEW_which_params: prediction error (|PE|), inference-dependent update (PE x responsibility interaction) from the HMMKF model
NEW_param_manipulation_link: dmPFC cTBS selectively impaired the inference-dependent (responsibility-modulated) update, increasing the effect of outcome on ratings for high-|PE| trials that should not be updated, while sparing |PE|-based inference itself (unchanged relative to vertex).
def_quote: Learning during social interaction entails both inferring the latent cause and updating the association between the observation and the cause.
research_question: How does the brain infer which of two co-acting characters (latent causes) was responsible for a jointly achieved outcome, and how does it then update the estimated association between the responsible character and that outcome? The study asks whether these two computations (inference vs. update) are dissociable and instantiated in distinct brain regions (hippocampus vs. dmPFC).
sl_operationalization: Participants observed outcomes ostensibly produced jointly by pairs of characters across trials and had to (1) infer which character was more responsible (latent-cause inference) and (2) update a Bayesian estimate of each character's ability/performance based on the outcome and the inferred responsibility, producing an asymmetric update (more updating of the estimate for whichever character was inferred as more responsible for good vs. bad outcomes). This inference-and-update process was modeled with a Bayesian learning model and tested against hippocampal (inference) and dmPFC (update) activity, with dmPFC causally implicated via cTBS.
